Separately, the European Commission said in preliminary findings that Temu’s product checks, moderation and seller penalties do not adequately reduce the risk of illegal or unsafe goods being sold to EU consumers. The platform has more than 120 million users in the bloc. The Commission’s inquiry also covers Temu’s recommendation systems, service design and access to data for researchers. Temu can examine the case file and respond in writing; the Commission will consult the European Board for Digital Services before deciding whether to confirm a breach and require corrective action.

items.title: [Fast Company] All these outages show how corporate America needs to modernize out-of-date tech
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Over the past five days, a string of high-profile tech outages has left Americans struggling to send emails, catch flights, and access their bank accounts.

While the disruptions raised concerns about AI-powered cybersecurity threats, the real culprit may be something less sinister: corporate America’s tech systems are simply out of date. 

Outages like those at JPMorgan Chase, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), and Microsoft can occur when computer systems are undergoing major upgrades, Marva Bailer, CEO of tech advisory firm Qualaix, told the New York Post. Bolting on new technology can leave the systems vulnerable.

Although it is unclear whether the recent outages were directly related to artificial intelligence, many organizations are currently upgrading their networks to handle AI tools. Microsoft attributed its outage to an issue that arose during a network capacity upgrade, according to the Financial Times.

The time of year could also be a factor, as technicians rush to make sure systems are ready for the holiday shopping and travel season.

“It’s holiday time, it’s travel time, it’s shopping,” Bailer told the New York Post. “So, you have all those higher spikes in volume and more pressure to [update your systems].”

AI is also allowing companies to identify software vulnerabilities far more quickly, possibly leaving IT workers with too much work on their hands, the Post reported.

Like Bailer, U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin attributed the disruptions to companies trying to upgrade aging systems, during an appearance on CNBC earlier today.

“[They’re] pushing new technology on top of really old computer systems, and it just seems to overwhelm the system,” he said.

The disruptions serve as a reminder of how cutting-edge technology is often still dependent on centralized, aging systems.

Friday’s nationwide ground stop, which resulted in more than 18,000 flight cancellations over three days, was triggered by the installation of a single router at a remote facility in Arkansas, Reuters reported. Monday’s software glitch at JPMorgan Chase disrupted transactions for customers of other major banks, even though their own computer systems were functioning normally.

Indeed, third-party tech providers have accounted for roughly two-thirds of publicly reported IT outages over the past nine years, according to a recent report from Uptime Institute, a global digital infrastructure advisory firm based in New York City.

items.title: [ArchDaily] UN-Habitat and ICPAC Launch a Practical Guide to Help Cities Prepare for El Niño
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

El Niño is a natural climate pattern expected to peak from October 2026 through March 2027. It is characterized by a strong impact on global weather patterns, bringing floods, droughts, heat waves and storms to different regions. On November 5, 2026, the United Nations Human Settlements Programme (UN-Habitat) and the Climate Prediction and Applications Centre (ICPAC) of the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) launched a short practical guide for city governments to help them prepare for the upcoming season. The guide offers considerations applicable to different climate regions, but it is framed by IGAD in the context of preparedness, anticipatory action and resilience in the Horn of Africa (Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Kenya, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan and Uganda). items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Astronomers say the hot Jupiter TOI-2535 b, about 1,000 light-years away, stopped transiting its star in March 2026 because the gravitational pull of a nearby, still-unseen planet tilted its orbit out of Earth’s line of sight. NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite observed the system from April 2019 to March 2026; the planet circles its star every 8.25 days. Before the transits vanished, they arrived as much as six hours early or late and grew shorter and shallower, signs that the orbit’s alignment was changing. How the planet moved close to its star remains uncertain. The study appeared in *The Astrophysical Journal Letters* on Nov. 9. TOI-2535 b is not expected to transit again for at least 30 years, while its companion could become visible in transit sooner.

U.S. households are projected to spend an average of $1,002 on home heating this winter, up 7.1%, or $66, from last year, according to the National Energy Assistance Directors Association (NEADA), which represents state officials seeking federal funding. Households using heating oil face the steepest increase, with average bills forecast at $2,977, up 70.2%. Electric heating costs are forecast to rise 6% and propane costs 5%, while natural-gas heating costs are expected to remain roughly unchanged. NEADA links the heating-oil forecast to supply disruptions from the war with Iran and uncertainty around the Strait of Hormuz. items.title: [nbcchicago.com] IRS raises 2027 tax brackets and child credit limits
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

The Internal Revenue Service raised federal income tax bracket thresholds for 2027, allowing taxpayers to earn more before entering a higher bracket. Tax rates remain unchanged, with the top rate still 37%. For single filers, the 22% bracket starts above $52,025 and the 37% bracket above $661,375; for married couples filing jointly, those thresholds are $104,050 and $793,650. The IRS also increased the maximum child tax credit to $2,300, including a refundable portion of up to $1,800, and raised the maximum earned income tax credit for qualifying families with at least three children to $8,496. The annual inflation adjustments are intended to keep wage increases from pushing taxpayers into higher brackets when their purchasing power has not increased.

items.title: [energynow.com] Goldman Sachs forecasts Brent to fall to $78 as 2027 surplus builds
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Goldman Sachs expects Brent crude to average $88 a barrel in 2027 and fall to $78 by December as the oil market shifts toward a surplus of 2 million barrels a day. It forecasts West Texas Intermediate (WTI) will average $78 in 2027 and end the year at $70. The bank sees near-term price risks from attacks on Middle East shipping and damage to oil infrastructure, but says stronger supply, weaker demand or a declining risk premium could pull prices lower later. Brent and WTI fell more than 3% on Monday, with Brent trading at $92.59, as traders weighed recovering shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and expectations of increased supply. The outlook is disputed. Dmitry Kasatkin, a partner at Kasatkin Consulting, said it was premature to forecast a lasting surplus while inventories were being depleted. Olga Osharova, a partner at S+ Consulting, put the current inventory shortfall at about 460 million barrels and estimated that a surplus of 2 million barrels a day would take seven to eight months to close the gap.

items.title: [euronews.com] Hungary seizes $19.5 million in cash during ex-minister probe
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Hungarian investigators recovered about $19.5 million in cash during searches tied to former National Development Minister Miklós Seszták, who served under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH), Hungary’s anti-corruption agency, said investigators found the money in forests, farm buildings, warehouses, homes and a remote safe, then deposited it with the state treasury. Prosecutors suspect Seszták and former Hungarian National Asset Management chief Norbert Szivek received more than 11 billion forints in illicit payments between 2015 and 2018 from companies connected to Volánbusz, Hungary’s state bus operator. The case includes alleged purchases of used buses at inflated prices. Seszták denies wrongdoing, and his lawyer says the seized money did not belong to him. The searches are part of Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s anti-corruption drive following his April election victory, which ended Orbán’s 16 years in power. A court extended Seszták’s pretrial detention until Jan. 30, 2027, citing the seriousness of the case and the risk that he might flee. NVVH president Anna Unger said investigators would continue their work.
